flashcards.q: Why must etcd clusters be sized odd (3 or 5), and what does a 4-node cluster actually get you?
flashcards.a: Quorum = floor(n/2)+1. 3 nodes need 2 (tolerate 1 failure), 5 need 3 (tolerate 2). A 4-node cluster also needs 3, giving the exact same fault tolerance as 3 nodes for extra replication/storage cost — never size even.

flashcards.q: What single component is the only one allowed to write to etcd, and how does it enforce write safety under concurrent updates?
flashcards.a: The API server. It uses optimistic concurrency via resourceVersion — a stale write (based on an outdated version) is rejected with HTTP 409 Conflict, forcing the client to re-fetch and retry.

flashcards.q: What does 'mvcc: database space exceeded' mean in etcd, and what's the correct two-step fix?
flashcards.a: etcd hit its backend size quota (default 2GB) and entered an alarm state rejecting all writes. Fix: compact old MVCC revisions (logical space) THEN defragment (reclaims disk space at the storage engine level) — compaction alone doesn't shrink the on-disk file.

flashcards.q: What are the scheduler's two sequential phases per pod, and what happens to a node that fails a Filter check?
flashcards.a: Filter (~14 in-tree plugins, e.g. NodeResourcesFit, taints/tolerations, PodTopologySpread) then Score (~9 in-tree plugins, 0-100 weighted sum, e.g. ImageLocality). A node failing ANY Filter check is dropped entirely and never reaches Score.

flashcards.q: What happens when no node passes Filter for a pending pod?
flashcards.a: PostFilter runs preemption: the scheduler looks for lower-priorityClassValue pods on some node whose eviction would free enough room, and if found, evicts them and retries scheduling that node for the pending pod.

flashcards.q: What does a Kubernetes controller's workqueue actually hold — full objects or something else — and why does that matter?
flashcards.a: Object keys (namespace/name), not full objects. This lets a rapid burst of updates to the same object collapse into a single dequeued key, and forces Reconcile to always re-fetch current state rather than trust potentially-stale event payload data.

flashcards.q: Why must a Reconcile function be idempotent?
flashcards.a: The same object key can be dequeued and reconciled multiple times for one logical change — at-least-once delivery, periodic resyncs, and restarts all cause repeat calls with no new information. Non-idempotent side effects (e.g. an external API call with no idempotency key) will double-fire.

flashcards.q: What's a common self-triggering infinite reconcile loop bug, and the fix?
flashcards.a: Calling Status().Update() unconditionally every Reconcile call — a status write is itself an object change that generates a new watch event, re-enqueueing the object and calling Reconcile again forever. Fix: deep-equal check current vs computed status before writing.

Controller is the general term for any reconcile loop (built-in controllers reconcile built-in types like Deployment/ReplicaSet). Operator specifically means a controller paired with a Custom Resource Definition, encoding domain-specific operational knowledge no built-in controller has.

flashcards.q: Why is leader election mandatory for a multi-replica custom controller?
flashcards.a: Without it, every replica's informer and reconcile loop runs independently and concurrently against the same objects, causing duplicate work and conflicting writes as replicas race each other. Leader election (via a Lease object) ensures only one replica actively reconciles at a time.

flashcards.q: What's a finalizer, and why doesn't kubectl delete always remove an object from etcd immediately?
flashcards.a: A string in metadata.finalizers. Deleting an object with finalizers present only sets deletionTimestamp; the object stays visible (terminating) until every finalizer is removed by its owning controller after it finishes cleanup (e.g. deprovisioning an external resource).

flashcards.q: Why must .status be recomputed from observation rather than tracked as remembered controller state?
flashcards.a: The controller process has no durability guarantee and can restart at any time with no memory of prior state; recomputing status from live observation on every Reconcile makes a restart invisible to correctness, since the next reconcile just derives true current state from scratch.
